tldr: By extending the front suspension and compressing the rear just before launching off a ramp, this study vastly expands the limits of mid-air attitude recovery, enabling stable landings even during extreme jumps that previously resulted in crashes.
hero_caption: The full-scale four-wheel independent drive vehicle and diverse ramp geometries evaluated in the experiments. (a) Series hydraulic suspension actuators are mounted at each wheel, and (b) evaluations were conducted across various conditions, including tabletop ramps, convex lips, and washboard rough terrain.
overview:
When a heavy off-road vehicle launches off a jump, the primary way to correct its mid-air pitch (fore-aft tilt) is reaction torque generated by accelerating or braking the wheels. However, because wheel rotational speed has a physical upper bound, attitude can only be corrected within the angular-momentum budget stored in the wheels. Prior work (DART) computed backward-reachable safe landing regions and adjusted approach speeds, but it could not actively reshape dangerous takeoff attitudes that exceeded the mid-air recovery budget.

Inspired by motocross riders preloading their suspension on jump faces, the authors propose "DART-S": a system that actively manipulates suspension before liftoff to simultaneously shape both the takeoff attitude and the residual wheel angular-momentum budget available in mid-air. By applying a nose-up suspension preset (front extended, rear compressed), the system modulates takeoff angle, pitch rate, and wheel spin to manage mid-air control authority.

Across 600 runs in the BeamNG.tech physics simulator, DART-S achieved 24/24 (100%) stable landings under an extreme boundary condition (40° ramp angle, 13 m/s approach speed) where baseline DART had a 0% success rate due to insufficient mid-air authority. Furthermore, the authors identified the nonlinear effect of suspension extension timing during liftoff, demonstrating that an appropriately timed intervention can prevent takeoff failures.
contributions: Redefining active suspension as a ramp-face attitude shaping actuator and establishing a two-sided reachability model that simultaneously alters both the takeoff pitch state and the airborne wheel angular-momentum budget.
Identifying non-monotonic dynamic behavior where attitude shifts reverse sign depending on suspension rebound and lip departure timing, establishing departure timing as an explicit control variable.
Developing an adaptive selector combining local outcome evidence, interval-reachability screening, and a convex-lip curvature safeguard to conservatively prevent unsafe interventions.

sections.heading: Can't fix your attitude in mid-air? Shape it before takeoff
sections.summary: Mid-air attitude control via wheel reaction torque faces hard physical limits imposed by maximum drivetrain speeds. DART-S overcomes this by using active suspension on the ramp face to optimize both takeoff attitude and mid-air control authority before liftoff.
sections.details:
When using wheel acceleration and braking reaction torque to control vehicle attitude in mid-air, recovery becomes impossible if the required correction exceeds the wheel angular-momentum budget. Prior work with DART revealed that for a 1383 kg vehicle, the maximum nose-up recoverable pitch rate is only about 9 to 13 deg/s. This limitation is not due to insufficient motor torque, but rather the drivetrain's rotational hard limit (approx. 221 rad/s), which caps the available angular momentum.

While DART computed reachable takeoff regions and could abort jumps or adjust approach speeds, it lacked ground-based actuators to directly force pitch and pitch rate into safe limits before liftoff. DART-S redefines per-wheel active suspension—an actuator increasingly present on modern production vehicles like BYD's DiSus—as a "takeoff-state actuator."

The core insight is that suspension actions alter takeoff pitch angle and pitch rate while also shifting individual wheel speeds, thereby reshaping the residual angular-momentum budget available in mid-air. Instead of merely moving the state within a fixed safe set, DART-S performs a "two-sided intervention" that simultaneously shifts the state and alters the authority budget. This formalizes the motocross technique of preloading suspension on ramp faces into an automated, reachability-audited control system.

sections.heading: The intersection of mid-air control and active suspension
sections.summary: Existing mid-air attitude control relies on wheel or tail reaction torque, while suspension control typically focuses on ride comfort or landing impact absorption. DART-S bridges this gap by directly linking ramp-face suspension actions to post-takeoff angular-momentum budgets.
sections.details:
Related work spans three main domains.

The first is mid-air attitude control using wheels or reaction wheels. Prior studies include jumping and balancing platforms using reaction wheels, tail pendulum maneuvers, and quadruped jump controllers. Vehicle wheel reaction torque has also been explored in simulation and hardware, but these methods focus primarily on airborne control and do not connect ramp-face suspension behavior to airborne angular-momentum budgets.

The second is active suspension control. From semi-active setups to modern fully active hydraulic systems, model predictive control (MPC) has been widely applied for terrain following and bump traversal. Jump-related automotive patents exist, but they focus on passive preparation after mid-air detection or drivetrain protection upon touchdown, without actively shaping takeoff attitudes on ramp faces.

The third is ramp-face state planning. Examples include motocross preload techniques, rallycross simulations stiffening rear dampers to mitigate rear kick, and contact-implicit trajectory optimization. However, none of these integrate ramp actions with reachability audits that account for residual wheel angular momentum during airborne flight. DART-S fills this missing link.

sections.heading: A two-stage architecture that reshapes state and budget simultaneously
sections.summary: By controlling suspension displacement and release timing on the ramp, DART-S uses a calibration map to predict takeoff state shifts and wheel budget changes. A decision selector combining interval reachability and local evidence guarantees safe interventions.
sections.details:
The DART-S pipeline consists of three phases: ground approach (P0), airborne flight (P1), and landing (P2).

### Takeoff State and Two-Sided Reachability Model
The takeoff state is defined as $x_0 = (v_0, \theta_0, \omega_{\theta 0}, \Omega_{1,0}, \dots, \Omega_{4,0})$, where $v_0$ is approach speed, $\theta_0$ is pitch angle, $\omega_{\theta 0}$ is pitch rate, and $\Omega_{i,0}$ are individual wheel speeds. Applying a suspension command $u = (+1, +1, -1, -1)$ (lifting the front wheels and lowering the rear in a nose-up preset) induces a static geometric pitch shift ($\Delta\theta_0$) along with a transient pitch-rate increment ($\Delta\omega_{\theta 0}$) when the front wheels clear the lip and unweight. Furthermore, normal load shifts alter wheel spin speeds, modifying the upward and downward angular-momentum budgets $B_\uparrow$ and $B_\downarrow$ available in mid-air.

### Calibration Maps and Timing Control
Because hydraulic suspension has non-negligible response delay, commands are dispatched on flat ground before entering the ramp. In addition to a static preset that holds attitude, DART-S introduces "timing control" that temporarily returns suspension toward neutral right before liftoff. When the time to the lip reaches $t_{\mathrm{lip}} \le t_{\mathrm{lead}}$, the preset is halved for a duration $T_{\mathrm{pulse}}$ (approx. 0.12 s) and redeployed just before takeoff. These effects are identified ahead of time using a local calibration map $\operatorname{CalMap}(g, v, a_s)$ conditioned on ramp geometry, speed, and suspension action.

### Reachability Auditing and Fallback
The online selector evaluates an interval-reachable set $\mathcal{F}_\theta^{\mathrm{int}}$ ensuring post-touchdown pitch and pitch rate remain within safe bounds. An intervention is permitted only when the unassisted state falls outside the reachable set while the preset state falls cleanly inside. Furthermore, the selector requires prior positive evidence under identical conditions and uniform safety across all four uncertainty corner bounds. On convex lips, centrifugal forces cause the vehicle to unweight early, extending rear-axle contact and inducing dangerous nose-down pitch rates (a collapse in normal acceleration margin $n(v) = g\cos\alpha - v^2/R$). When this margin drops below a threshold, the preset is rejected, falling back to standard DART control.

sections.heading: Rigorous statistical validation in a soft-body physics engine
sections.summary: Using the high-fidelity vehicle simulator BeamNG.tech, tests were conducted with a 1383 kg four-wheel independent drive vehicle. Data from 600 runs across 8 independent sessions were evaluated under strict hypothesis testing and drivetrain safety bounds.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted in BeamNG.tech (v0.38.3.0), which provides high-fidelity vehicle dynamics and deformation modeling. The target vehicle is a four-wheel independent drive system (4WIDS) with a mass of 1383 kg and pitch inertia $I_{yy} \approx 2043\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$. Each suspension unit incorporates a series hydraulic actuator with approximately 50 mm stroke (15% of nominal length), driven at a slew rate of 2 $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ (full stroke in roughly 0.5 s).

Ramp profiles included planar tabletop slopes (35° and 40° inclinations) and convex kicker ramps with circular lips (radii $R=35\,\mathrm{m}$ and $22\,\mathrm{m}$). Approach speeds were systematically evaluated between 9 and 19.5 m/s.

Performance metrics included a "first-contact criterion" (pitch within 35° and roll within 30° at touchdown) and a stricter "post-touchdown attitude criterion ($C_{\mathrm{post}}$)," requiring the vehicle to avoid rollover (pitch exceeding 85° or roll exceeding 80°) for 2 seconds post-landing.

To prevent simulator state contamination, the simulator was restarted across 8 independent sessions, each evaluating 3 repeated runs (24 runs per condition). Statistical significance was assessed using session-level sign-flip tests with Holm adjustment for strict reproducibility. An online command guard capped wheel speed requests at 200 rad/s to guarantee that the vehicle never exceeded its physical drivetrain hard limit (221.2 rad/s).

sections.heading: 100% success at boundary limits and overcoming the mid-speed trough
sections.summary: At the extreme 40°/13 m/s boundary where DART failed completely (0/24), DART-S achieved a flawless 24/24 success rate. Moreover, timing control resolved a non-monotonic release trough where suspension effects inverted depending on liftoff timing.
sections.details:
### Boundary Performance Comparison
Under the harshest tabletop condition (40° ramp angle, 13 m/s approach speed), baseline DART suffered from insufficient airborne recovery authority, achieving 0 successes across 24 runs. In contrast, DART-S cleared the post-touchdown attitude criterion in all 24 runs (100% success rate, $p=0.0234$). It similarly achieved 23 to 24 successes at 35°/15 m/s and 35°/16 m/s, proving decisive advantages along reachability boundaries. Thanks to the 200 rad/s guard, drivetrain hard-limit exceedance (221.2 rad/s) was zero across all 600 runs.

### Non-Monotonic Speed Response and the 11.5 m/s Trough
A static nose-up suspension preset did not always produce a nose-up attitude shift. On a 35° tabletop ramp, varying speed from 10 to 13 m/s revealed touch-down pitch shifts of +13.20° at 10 m/s and +2.85° at 11 m/s, but inverted to negative shifts of -1.35° at 11.5 m/s and -3.00° at 12 m/s—a release-phase trough where the preset worsened pitch.

Dissecting the cause revealed that while static pitch angle always gained +2° or more, the transient pitch rate when front wheels left the lip dropped to near zero (+0.5 to 0.0 deg/s) around 11.5–12 m/s. Suspension rebound timing destructively interfered with lip transit time, canceling the desired effect. Because simple speed interpolation breaks down here, localized decisions accounting for this nonlinearity are essential.

### Dramatic Recovery via Timing Control
To address this 11.5 m/s trough, a "0.35 s timing action" was introduced, briefly releasing the preset 0.35 s before lip departure. While the static preset achieved 0/24 successes, timing control vaulted performance to 23/24 ($p=0.0156$). Releasing suspension at the proper moment eliminated destructive interference and generated the intended corrective pitch rate.

### Convex Lip Dynamics and Safeguards
On convex kickers ($R=35\,\mathrm{m}$) at high speeds (18 m/s), front wheels unweighted early while rear wheels remained planted on the ramp for 0.36 s, pivoting the vehicle forward into a severe nose-down rotation (-9.1 deg/s). Enforcing a safeguard that blocks presets whenever normal acceleration margin drops below $n(v) \le 2\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ reliably rejected these harmful interventions.

sections.heading: Ramp-face preparation unlocks extreme off-road maneuvers
sections.summary: By treating active suspension as a ramp-face state and budget shaping actuator and coupling it with reachability audits, DART-S substantially pushes the operating boundaries of vehicle jumps.
sections.details:
This work presented DART-S, which employs active suspension on jump ramps as an actuator for both initial state and mid-air angular-momentum budgets. By preparing takeoff attitude and wheel speed reserves while still on the ground, the mid-air control loop can make full use of remaining authority, surviving severe jumps that were previously irrecoverable.

BeamNG simulations following rigorous statistical protocols validated 100% success at the 40°/13 m/s boundary and dramatic recoveries via timing control at 11.5 m/s. The system also demonstrated principled avoidance of nose-down pitching on curved lips using normal acceleration constraints.

Future research directions include physical hydraulic force measurements under high loads, sub-scale vehicle jump experiments, mitigating structural peak loads on the chassis, and extending reachability-audited preconditioning to full 3D spatial attitude control, including roll dynamics.

takeaways: When an actuator faces tight control authority (budget) limits, a two-sided design that reshapes both the initial state and the budget itself during a preceding phase is highly effective.
Even slow actuators like suspension can serve as potent angular-rate generators if transient ground-release dynamics (rebound timing and unweighting) are harnessed correctly.
Suspension preset responses can be non-monotonic with respect to speed (exhibiting inverted troughs), necessitating local evidence-based screening rather than naive linear interpolation.
limitations: Evaluations remain confined to BeamNG.tech physics simulations, lacking physical hardware validation regarding hydraulic response delays, transient tire carcass compliance, and chassis structural stress limits.
Control focuses exclusively on the pitch axis; actively managing coupled roll and yaw dynamics caused by asymmetric ramps or uneven approaches remains an open challenge.
Outside the domain of the local calibration map (CalMap), the system must fall back to baseline DART, limiting generalization across arbitrary, unmapped ramp geometries.
